prompt: [Co(NH3)4(H2O)Cl]Cl2 and [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl·H2O have the same overall composition. What type of isomers are they?

choices.text: Hydrate isomers
Linkage isomers
choices.why: Linkage isomers differ in which atom of an ambidentate ligand binds. Here a water and a chloride swap between ligand and lattice/counterion roles.

choices.text: Coordination isomers
choices.why: Coordination isomers need two complex ions swapping ligands. There is only one complex here.

choices.text: Geometric isomers
choices.why: Geometric isomers have the same ligands in different arrangements. Here the ligand sets themselves differ.

explanation: Hydrate (solvate) isomers differ in whether water acts as a ligand or as lattice water (a hydrate), and correspondingly in whether a potential counterion is a ligand or a counterion. In the first compound, water is an aqua ligand; in the second, it is lattice water and a second chloride is bound instead.

prompt: [Pt(NH3)4Cl2]Br2 and [Pt(NH3)4Br2]Cl2 differ only in which anions are bound to platinum and which are counterions. What type of isomerism is this?

choices.text: Ionization isomerism
Hydrate isomerism
choices.why: Hydrate isomers differ in whether water is a ligand or lattice water. No water is involved here.

choices.text: Linkage isomerism
choices.why: Linkage isomers involve one ambidentate ligand binding through different atoms. Here different ions are bound.

choices.text: Optical isomerism
choices.why: These compounds have different ligand sets, not mirror-image arrangements of the same ligands.

explanation: In ionization isomerism, two or more ions could act as ligands, and the isomers differ in which ones are ligands and which are counterions. Here chloride is bound in one compound and bromide in the other.

prompt: [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Br and [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 are ionization isomers. How many moles of AgBr precipitate when excess Ag^+ is added to a solution containing 1 mol of [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Br?
explanation: In [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Br the sulfate is bound to cobalt and the one bromide is a free counterion, so 1 mol of Br^− precipitates as 1 mol AgBr. Its isomer [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 has its bromide bound and would give none.

prompt: [Cu(NH3)4][PtCl4] and [Pt(NH3)4][CuCl4] contain the same metals and ligands. What type of isomers are they?

choices.text: Coordination isomers
Ionization isomers
choices.why: Ionization isomers swap ligands with a simple counterion. Here two complex ions trade ligand sets.

choices.text: Linkage isomers
choices.why: No ligand changes its donor atom; NH3 and Cl^− move between metals.

choices.text: Enantiomers
choices.why: Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images with the same connectivity. Here the ligands are on different metals.

explanation: Coordination isomers occur in compounds containing two or more complexes whose ligands could be swapped between them. Moving the NH3 ligands from Cu to Pt and the Cl^− from Pt to Cu gives the coordination isomer, just as [Co(NH3)6][Cr(ox)3] relates to [Cr(NH3)6][Co(ox)3].

prompt: [Co(NH3)5(SCN)]^2+ and [Co(NH3)5(NCS)]^2+ differ only in whether thiocyanate binds cobalt through S or through N. What type of isomers are they?

choices.text: Linkage isomers
Ionization isomers
choices.why: No ion moves between the coordination sphere and the counterion position.

choices.text: Geometric isomers
choices.why: With a single thiocyanate there is no cis/trans relationship to change. The donor atom changes.

choices.text: Coordination isomers
choices.why: Coordination isomers need two complexes that swap ligands.

explanation: Linkage (ambidentate) isomers differ in how an ambidentate ligand binds the metal. Thiocyanate can bind through S or N, so its complexes can exist as linkage isomers, and which one forms has to be determined experimentally.

prompt: Which of these ligands cannot give rise to linkage isomers?

choices.text: NH3
CN^−
choices.why: Cyanide is ambidentate: it can bind through C or N, though it usually binds through C.

choices.text: NO2^−
choices.why: Nitrite is ambidentate: it binds through N (nitro) or O (nitrito).
Sulfite is on the section's list of ambidentate ligands that give linkage isomerism.

explanation: The main ambidentate ligands are cyanide, thiocyanate (and OCN^− and SeCN^−), nitrite, sulfite, and nitrosyl. NH3 has only one donor atom, its nitrogen lone pair, so it can bind in only one way.

prompt: Cyanide can bridge two metals as M–C≡N–M'. In Prussian blue, how are the cyanide bridges oriented between Fe(II) and Fe(III)?

choices.text: Carbon binds Fe(II) and nitrogen binds Fe(III): Fe^{II}–C≡N–Fe^{III}
Nitrogen binds Fe(II) and carbon binds Fe(III)
choices.why: This is reversed. In Prussian blue the linkages are Fe^{II}–C≡N–Fe^{III}.

choices.text: Both ends of each cyanide bind the same iron atom
choices.why: A bridging cyanide links two different metal centers, one at each end.

choices.text: Cyanide binds only through carbon, so it can't bridge
choices.why: Cyanide usually binds through C but can also use its N end, letting it bridge two metals.

explanation: Some ambidentate ligands can bind two different metals at once, linking them. Cyanide forms M–C≡N–M' linkages, and in the dye Prussian blue these take the form Fe^{II}–C≡N–Fe^{III}.

prompt: What happens when the yellow nitro complex [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]^2+, with nitrite bound through N, is irradiated with light?

choices.text: It converts to the less stable red O-bound nitrito linkage isomer, [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]^2+
It converts to a more stable O-bound isomer
choices.why: The nitro (N-bound) form is the thermodynamically more stable one; light drives it to the less stable nitrito form.

choices.text: It releases free NO2^− as an ionization isomer forms
choices.why: The nitrite stays bound; only its donor atom changes from N to O.

choices.text: It converts from cis to trans
choices.why: With one nitrite and five NH3 there is no cis/trans pair. The change is in the linkage.

explanation: Some ambidentate ligands can be switched from one binding mode to another by a stimulus. The classic example is light converting the thermodynamically more stable yellow nitro complex [Co(NH3)5NO2]^2+ to the less stable red O-nitrito complex [Co(NH3)5ONO]^2+.

prompt: Which point group would a chiral coordination complex have?

choices.text: D3
D4h
choices.why: D4h, typical of square planar complexes, contains mirror planes and an inversion center, so it is achiral.

choices.text: C2v
choices.why: C2v has mirror planes, so a molecule with this symmetry is superimposable on its mirror image.

choices.text: Oh
choices.why: Oh contains mirror planes and an inversion center: achiral.

explanation: Molecules with only proper rotation axes, meaning point groups Dn, Cn, or C1, are chiral and show optical isomerism. Octahedral tris-chelates like [V(ox)3]^3− have D3 symmetry and exist as Λ and Δ enantiomers.

prompt: Why is a square planar complex with four different ligands not chiral, even though a tetrahedral one can be?

choices.text: The plane of the molecule is a mirror plane, so the complex is superimposable on its mirror image
Square planar metals cannot bind four different ligands
choices.why: They can; the point is that such a complex is identical to its mirror image.

choices.text: Square planar complexes always racemize instantly
choices.why: There's nothing to racemize: the complex has a mirror plane and is achiral (point group Cs).

choices.text: Only octahedral complexes can be chiral
choices.why: Tetrahedral Mabcd complexes can be chiral too, like a carbon stereocenter.

explanation: A four-coordinate complex must have tetrahedral geometry to be chiral like a carbon stereocenter. A square planar Mabcd complex has all four ligands in one plane, which is a mirror plane (point group Cs), so it is the same as its mirror image.

prompt: Tetrahedral Mabcd complexes with simple monodentate ligands are chiral in principle. Why are their enantiomers often hard or impossible to resolve?

choices.text: Their metal–ligand bonds are weaker and more flexible than C–C bonds, so the enantiomers tend to interconvert by a fluxional process
They are actually achiral because of a mirror plane
choices.why: A true tetrahedral center with four different ligands has no mirror plane; the problem is interconversion.

choices.text: Enantiomers of metal complexes don't rotate polarized light
choices.why: Chiral complexes are optically active. The difficulty is that these enantiomers interconvert.

choices.text: They always crystallize as square planar complexes
choices.why: The issue the section describes is fluxional interconversion, not a geometry change on crystallization.

explanation: Metal–ligand bonds to sterically unhindered monodentate ligands are generally weaker and more flexible than C–C bonds, so the enantiomers would likely interconvert. Such chirality is most easily realized with macrocyclic ligands like proteins.

prompt: A chiral secondary amine like ethylmethylamine racemizes rapidly as a free molecule. What changes when it binds to a metal?

choices.text: Nitrogen inversion is frozen out, so its R and S forms no longer interconvert
It loses its chirality because the lone pair is used
choices.why: When bound, the N has four different groups (including the metal), so it's still a stereocenter, now without inversion.

choices.text: It racemizes even faster
choices.why: Binding stops nitrogen inversion rather than speeding it up.

choices.text: It becomes an ambidentate ligand
choices.why: The amine still binds only through N. The change is that its configuration gets locked.

explanation: Nitrogen inversion rapidly racemizes free chiral amines, but it is frozen out when the nitrogen bonds to a metal. Bound chiral amines therefore form non-interconverting R and S enantiomers, which also creates new possibilities for diastereomers.

prompt: What do the labels Λ and Δ describe for an octahedral tris-chelate such as [Cr(ox)3]^3−?

choices.text: The two enantiomers: Λ has the twist of a left-handed pinwheel, Δ that of a right-handed one
The two conformations of a single five-membered chelate ring
choices.why: Those are lowercase λ and δ, which describe ring twist.

choices.text: Whether three ligands lie on a face or in a plane
choices.why: That distinction is fac vs. mer.

choices.text: Whether two ligands are adjacent or opposite
choices.why: That distinction is cis vs. trans.

explanation: Octahedral tris-chelates have D3 symmetry and are chiral, existing as Λ and Δ enantiomers. Their chirality is like a pinwheel's: the Λ enantiomer has the symmetry of a left-handed pinwheel and the Δ enantiomer that of a right-handed one.

prompt: How many stereoisomers does the octahedral tris-chelate [Cr(ox)3]^3− have? (Ignore chelate ring twist.)
explanation: With three identical symmetric chelates, there is no cis/trans or fac/mer choice. The complex has D3 symmetry, which is chiral, so it exists as one pair of enantiomers, Λ and Δ: 2 stereoisomers.

prompt: How many stereoisomers does octahedral [Cr(ox)2(H2O)2]^− have, counting enantiomers separately? (Ignore chelate ring twist.)
explanation: The two aqua ligands can be trans or cis. Trans is achiral (1). In the cis form, the complex is an octahedral bis-chelate M(L~L)2X2 with C2 symmetry, which is chiral, so it exists as Λ and Δ (2). Total: 1 + 2 = 3.

prompt: How many stereoisomers does octahedral [Co(NH3)3Cl2(H2O)]^+ have?
explanation: Start with the three NH3. If they're fac, the Cl, Cl, and H2O fill the opposite face, and all such placements are the same: 1 isomer. If they're mer, one remaining site is trans to an NH3 and the other two are trans to each other: either the two Cl are trans (H2O trans to NH3), or one Cl is trans to NH3 and the other trans to H2O: 2 isomers. None is chiral, so the total is 3.

prompt: How many stereoisomers does octahedral [Co(en)(NH3)3Cl]^2+ have? (Ignore chelate ring twist.)
explanation: The en must span two cis positions. Focus on the unique ligand, Cl: it can be trans to one of the en nitrogens, or trans to an NH3. Each arrangement has a mirror plane, so neither is chiral. Total: 2.

prompt: How many isomers does the square planar Pt(II) complex [Pt(NH3)2BrCl] have?
explanation: Square planar complexes can show cis/trans isomerism. The two NH3 can be cis (90°) or trans (180°); once that's fixed, Br and Cl fill the remaining two sites in only one distinct way. The molecular plane is a mirror plane, so neither is chiral. Total: 2.

prompt: Glycinate (gly^−) is an unsymmetrical bidentate ligand that binds through one N and one O on cis positions. How many stereoisomers does octahedral [Cr(gly)2(H2O)2]^+ have, counting enantiomers separately? (Ignore chelate ring twist.)
explanation: Waters trans: both gly lie in the equatorial plane, with their O ends either cis or trans to each other. That plane is a mirror plane, so these are 2 achiral isomers. Waters cis: each water is trans to a gly donor atom, giving three cases (both trans to O, both trans to N, one of each). Each is a cis bis-chelate, so each is chiral (Λ and Δ): 3 × 2 = 6. Total: 2 + 6 = 8.

prompt: In the MABCDEF bookkeeping method, isomers are listed by their sets of trans pairs. How many distinct sets of trans pairs (geometric arrangements, before considering enantiomers) are possible for an octahedral MA2BCDE complex?
explanation: Case 1: the two A ligands trans to each other. B, C, D, E then pair up as BC/DE, BD/CE, or BE/CD: 3 sets. Case 2: each A is trans to a different one of B–E. Choose which two: C(4,2) = 6 ways, and the remaining two must be trans to each other: 6 sets. Total: 3 + 6 = 9.

prompt: In the MABCDEF bookkeeping system, multidentate ligands are classified first, with letters reflecting their attachment points. How is [Cr(gly)2(H2O)2]^+ classified, where gly binds through one N and one O?

choices.text: M(AB)2C2
M(AA)2B2
choices.why: AA is for a chelate with identical attachment points, like en. Glycinate has two different donor atoms, so it is AB.

choices.text: MA2B2C2
choices.why: That would treat every donor as a separate monodentate ligand and lose the information that each gly spans two sites.

choices.text: M(ABBA)C2
choices.why: ABBA describes a single tetradentate ligand like trien, not two separate glycinates.

explanation: Multidentate ligands are classified before monodentate ones and labeled by the symmetry of their attachment points: en is AA and gly, with a carboxylate O and an amine N, is AB. So [CoCl2(en)2]^+ is M(AA)2B2 and a bis(glycinato) complex with two identical monodentate ligands is M(AB)2C2.

prompt: What is the oxidation state of iron in the neutral complex [Fe(salen)Cl], where salen binds as a 2− ligand?
explanation: Treat each ligand as its charge when bound: x + (−2) + (−1) = 0, so x = +3.

prompt: Why can square planar complexes show cis/trans isomerism while tetrahedral complexes cannot?

choices.text: In a tetrahedron every position is adjacent to every other, so there is no pair of positions opposite each other (180°)
Tetrahedral complexes have only three ligands
choices.why: Tetrahedral complexes have four ligands, but all at 109.5° to one another.

choices.text: Tetrahedral metals can only bind identical ligands
choices.why: Tetrahedral complexes can carry different ligands; with four different ones they are even chiral.

choices.text: Square planar complexes have 120° angles
choices.why: Square planar complexes have 90° (cis) and 180° (trans) L–M–L angles, the same relationships as in an octahedron.

explanation: Cis ligands are adjacent, with an L–M–L angle of 90°; trans ligands are on opposite sides, at 180°. Square planar and octahedral centers have both relationships, so they show cis/trans isomerism. In a tetrahedron all four positions are equivalent and mutually adjacent, so no cis/trans pair exists.

prompt: Why does a square planar complex of the type [M(en)X2] exist only as the cis isomer?

choices.text: The two nitrogens of the chelating en can only span adjacent (cis) positions, which forces the two X ligands to be cis as well
Because en is a monodentate ligand
choices.why: en is bidentate; both nitrogens bind, and they can only reach neighboring sites.

choices.text: Because trans isomers are never possible in square planar complexes
choices.why: Many square planar complexes, like [PtCl2(NH3)2], exist as both cis and trans isomers.

choices.text: Because the X ligands repel each other into cis positions
choices.why: It's the chelate's geometry, not repulsion, that forces the cis arrangement.

explanation: A chelating ligand like en can only bind in a cis arrangement, so multidentate ligands can constrain a complex's geometry. PtCl2(en), for example, exists only as the cis isomer.

prompt: In a mer isomer of an octahedral MA3B3 complex, how are the three A ligands arranged?

choices.text: In one plane through the metal, forming a T shape, with two of them trans to each other
On one triangular face of the octahedron, all cis to one another
choices.why: That is the fac (facial) arrangement.

choices.text: All three trans to one another
choices.why: Only two positions can be trans to each other. Three ligands can't be mutually trans.

choices.text: At the corners of a tetrahedron around the metal
choices.why: The ligands sit at octahedral positions; mer and fac describe how three of them relate.

explanation: In the fac (facial) arrangement the three ligands occupy one face of the octahedron. In the mer (meridional) arrangement they form a T shape in one plane, or meridian, so two of them are trans.

prompt: For octahedral and square planar complexes, which chelate ring size tends to be especially stable?

choices.text: Five-membered rings, which suit the 90° L–M–L angles between cis positions
Three-membered rings
choices.why: These aren't among the common sizes; four-, five-, and six-membered rings are common, with five-membered rings favored here.

choices.text: Six-membered rings, as in the comparison with [Ni(en)3]^2+
choices.why: [Ni(en)3]^2+, with five-membered rings, has the higher overall formation constant than the six-membered-ring analog.

choices.text: Seven-membered rings
choices.why: Larger rings are more often needed for the wider angles of tetrahedral or trigonal bipyramidal centers.

explanation: Four-, six-, and especially five-membered chelate rings are common. With 90° angles between cis ligands, five-membered rings tend to be especially stable, which is reflected in the higher β3 of [Ni(en)3]^2+ compared to a six-membered-ring analog. The larger angles of tetrahedral and trigonal bipyramidal centers often call for six- or seven-membered rings.

prompt: What does λ/δ isomerism (lowercase) describe in metal complexes?

choices.text: The two twist conformations of a nonplanar five-membered chelate ring, such as one formed by en
The Λ and Δ enantiomers of an octahedral tris-chelate
choices.why: Those use capital Λ and Δ. Lowercase λ and δ describe the twist of an individual chelate ring.

choices.text: Which donor atom of an ambidentate ligand is bound
choices.why: That is linkage isomerism, shown with κ.

choices.text: Whether a chelate ring is planar or nonplanar
choices.why: Only nonplanar rings show λ/δ twist; the labels distinguish the two twisted forms.

explanation: Chelates with tetrahedral ring atoms, like en and dppe, form kinked, nonplanar rings. A five-membered ring can be seen as a planar L–M–L unit plus an E–E bar twisted above or below that plane, giving the two most stable conformers, λ and δ. These are flexible but not always rapidly interconverting, so they can be a source of diastereomerism.

prompt: What does a circular dichroism (CD) spectrum plot as a function of wavelength?

choices.text: Δε = εl − εr, the difference in extinction coefficients for left and right circularly polarized light
The total absorbance of unpolarized light
choices.why: That is an ordinary absorption spectrum. CD measures the difference in absorption of left and right circularly polarized light.

choices.text: The angle of optical rotation
choices.why: Optical rotation versus wavelength is optical rotatory dispersion (ORD), a different technique.

choices.text: The difference in refractive index between two solvents
choices.why: CD compares how a chiral sample absorbs left versus right circularly polarized light.

explanation: Chiral molecules absorb left and right circularly polarized light differently. CD spectra plot Δε = εl − εr against wavelength. The signs of the features depend on the enantiomer, and the CD spectra of two enantiomers mirror each other.

prompt: According to the Cotton effect, what happens to the optical rotation of a chiral complex near the absorption maximum of one of its chromophores?

choices.text: It changes sign, with the direction of the change depending on the configuration
It becomes zero at all wavelengths
choices.why: The rotation passes through zero as it changes sign at the absorption maximum; it isn't zero everywhere.

choices.text: It is the same for both enantiomers
choices.why: Enantiomers show opposite behavior: one gives a positive Cotton effect, the other a negative one.

choices.text: It stays constant, since optical rotation doesn't depend on wavelength
choices.why: Optical rotatory dispersion is exactly the measurement of how rotation changes with wavelength.

explanation: In optical rotatory dispersion (ORD), the rotation changes sign at the absorption maximum of a chromophore (the Cotton effect). For one configuration it goes from negative to positive with increasing wavelength (a positive Cotton effect); the other configuration shows the opposite, negative Cotton effect.

prompt: Why is CD spectroscopy especially convenient for studying optically active coordination complexes, compared with most chiral organic molecules?

choices.text: Complexes have low-energy electronic transitions in the near UV and visible range
Complexes don't absorb light, so only their rotation matters
choices.why: Just the opposite: complexes absorb in the near UV and visible, which is what CD exploits.

choices.text: Only coordination complexes can be chiral
choices.why: Chiral organic molecules are common; they just usually lack these low-energy transitions.

choices.text: CD gives the same spectrum for both enantiomers, which simplifies analysis
choices.why: The CD spectra of enantiomers are mirror images. That difference is what makes CD useful for assigning configuration.

explanation: Unlike most chiral organics, optically active complexes have low-energy electronic transitions in the near UV and visible. So their different absorption and refraction of left and right circularly polarized light can reveal both their configuration and their electronic structure.
